ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS 
Enactment of legislation to administer food laws under a single 
authority 
*61. SHRI RS. GAVAI: Will the Minister of AGRICULTURE be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government propose to enact legislation to create a 
single authority to administer all the food laws under one umbrella; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) efforts made by Government for creation of infrastructure like 
cold chains, warehouses, transportation, etc. for food processing 
sector; 
(d) whemer Food Processing Sector is facing negative growth rate 
during last two years; and 
(e) if so, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE (SHRI NITISH 
KUMAR): (a) to (e) A Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) and (b) Department of Food Processing Industries (DFPI) 
organized four regional Seminars at  Calcutta, Mumbai, Bangalore and 
Lucknow to elicit regional inputs towards formulation of National 
Food Processing Policy. In these seminars, mere was a general 
consensus that apart from formulation of a national policy on food 
processing, an appropriate development oriented legislation be 
conceived as the present enactments are impeding the growth of the 
sector. Accordingly, an Approach Paper towards formulation of a 
Processed 
1 

RAJYA SABHA [23 November, 2000] 
food Development Act has been prepared and circulated* to various Central 
Government Departments, State Governments, Industry Associations, 
Research & Development Organizations and Experts. A copy of the same is 
attached as Statement-I. (See below) 
(c) The Government has taken a number of policy initiative to 
promote the growth of processed food sector in the country which include 
inter alia provision of financial assistance in the form of soft loan and 
grant to private industries, public sector undertakings, non-government 
organizations, cooperatives etc. Such  assistance is also provided for 
creation of infrastructure facilities. 
(d) and (e) Food Processing Industries cover different segments of 
this sector and a negative growth rate for the whole sector is not report. 
However, in Fruit & Vegetable Processing Sector, during the year 1997-98, 
the growth showed a negative trend. Though detailed reasons for this trend 
have not been reported, one of the apparently discernible factors to which the 
negative growth could be attributed is levying of excise duty on these 
products as against the zero duty in the preceding years. 
Statement-I 
Approach paper on proposed processed food development Act 
In 1995, the Government of India appointed a Task Force under the 
chairmanship of Justice (Retd.) E.S. Venketaramaiah to review the existing 
Food Laws including Prevention of Food Adulteration Act (PFA Act) and 
to suggest a simplified and harmonized Food Law. This Task Force opined 
that there should be a paradigm shift in the legal framework to promote 
good manufacturing practices' which has been universally found to be a 
better instrument to protect public health, minimize commercial fraud and to 
promote the development of industry and trade on scientific lines. The Prime 
Minister's Council on Trade and Industry appointed a Subject Group on 
Food and Agro Industries headed by Nusli Wadia. This group recommended 
that there is an urgent need to not only avoid existing multiplicity of laws 
and multi farious agencies administering them but also suggested that 
the harmonization of these laws under a single umbrella so that a single 
authority can supervise the effective implementation of the law concerning 
food sector. An unwieldy number of laws pervade this industry. Some of 
them specific to the sector and others affecting the sector indirectly. A list 
of various laws is appended is Statement-I! to this Paper, from which it can 
be discerned that the food industry 
2 

[23 November, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
is inexorably bound by the different co-ordinates of a wide ranging 
enactments. (See below) These Acts are oblivious of various 
developments in science, disciplines of food micro-biology, food 
chemistry, food technology and various trade developments that have 
taken place in the last few years. 
The Committee of Secretaries in its meeting held on 31 st May, 
1999 also underscored the prim e need for rationalization and 
simplification of the various food laws and also directed that food 
standards be determined and administered by a single authority. 
This Department recently organized four regional seminars to elicit 
inputs for drafting the National Food Processing Policy. The industry 
representatives were particularly of the view that the existing food laws 
have been impeding their growth since many times it is not possible 
for them to keep track of requirements of different Acts and that they 
are caught in the throes of multi-pronged enactments requiring enormous 
time and money on their part to conform to the requirements. The 
existing laws were framed to take car e of different situations and these 
are essentially regulatory in character. As such, these do not in any 
way help in the development process. The industry also raised several 
other issues during the Regional Seminars. One issue relates to the 
WTO challenges including import of food items from other countries 
into India, the items which are otherwise considered waste in the 
country of origin. It was also desired that the proposed Act should 
cover aspects such as micro-nutrients and food fortification, import of 
new technologies such as genetically modified foods, export 
regulations, standards, merit goods, taxation etc. They also emphasized 
the need for futures market and suggested creation of enabling 
environment for attracting huge investments in this sector. 
Government assistance by means of appropriate fund and also by 
creation of network of laboratories and R&D organizations, it was felt, 
would go a long way in gearing the industry to become competitive in 
the international arena. It is felt that there is an urgent need to bring in a 
new legislation entitled Processed Food Development Act which will 
take into account the core elements of existing food laws that are 
relevant to the present day context and also introduce other provisions 
to cater to the industry's requirements. 
Contents of the Proposed Act 
The proposed Act when introduced is expected to provide a single 
window system and will move from regulatory penal regime to that of 
promotional and developmental mech anism so as to sub serve the 
interest of the Indian food 
3 

RAJYA SABHA [23 November, 2000] 
industry and to make them viable and competitive to derive the best 
advantage of globalization of markets. 
The proposed Act will attempt to harmonize and rationalize the 
existing food laws. An attempt will also be made to simplify the rules 
and procedures so as to make it easy for the industry to comply with the 
requirements. These provisions w ill also take into account the 
requirements of sanitary and phyto sanitary measures required to be 
adopted as per international standards of manufacturing practices. 
An appropriate provision will be made for defining standards. 
This provision will cover not only the nationally manufactured goods 
but also the imported goods. The definition and standards will take into 
account the provisions of AGMARK, Export (Quality Control & 
Inspection) Act, ISO-9000, SQS-2000 besides Codex standards. The 
standards defined in the proposed Act will be a compulsory provision 
rather than the existing voluntary submission. The powers of checking 
and certification will be given to a network of laboratories and R&D 
institutions who are considered to po ssess necessary infrastructure in 
this regard. 
It is also envisaged to provide for an authority who would not 
only oversee the implementation of the standards but will also have 
powers to guide and rectify the manufacturing practices as well as to 
suggest the requisite methodology for adoption by the industry/unit 
concerned. The decision of mis authority will be final and binding and 
there will be no appeal provision against the decision of this authority. 
This authority will be a compact Committee consisting of industry 
representatives, representatives of national laboratories, R&D 
organizations who are conversant with standards and limited 
Government representatives so that the compliance will be readily 
forthcoming to its decision. 
Since the emphasis of the Act will be on development, it is 
proposed to include certain provisions for grant of incentives. In this 
regard, the Act will propose to define what are merit goods and the kind 
of incentives that could be made for manufacturers of such merit goods. 
The merit goods will be defined in terms of value addition and higher 
the value addition the more will be the incentives. An enabling 
provision for providing similar incentives with regard to products from 
difficult and backward areas will be incorporated to treat them on par 
with merit goods. It is also proposed to appropriately make provisions 
for setting up a Development Fund for the Food Processing Industry to 
enable the sector to have ready access to investible fund at a reasonable 
capital cost. 
4 

[23 November, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
It is also proposed to set up an Equalization Fund under this Act. 
It is observed that in the food proc essing sector, the cost of production 
fluctuates depending upon a variety of factors such as cost of raw 
material, cost of technology, marketing infrastructure and others. At 
times, it is likely that the sale pro ceeds may fall below the cost and the 
industry will suffer adversely. In such a situation, the differential 
between the cost price and the sale proceed will be made available to 
the industry from the Equalization Fund. Where a lot of surplus is 
expected from the sale proceeds, a portion of surplus will go back to the 
Fund as a means of replenishment of the Fund. 
Ministry of Environment have already issued a Notification 
regarding manufacture, use, import/export and storage of genetically 
engineered organisms of cells. The proposed Act, however, will contain 
enabling provisions for regulating the genetically engineered or 
modified food items either by means of compulsory labeling or in 
certain cases totally banning such items either from being imported into 
the country or from being manufactured or sold in the country. 
Appropriate rules will be made with reference to these provisions so that 
such food items which may have long term deleterious effects, can be 
controlled.

Rationalisation of Labour Laws 
*62. SHRI P. PRABHAKAR REDD Y: Will the Minister of 
LABOUR be pleased to state; 
(a) whether Government have set up a National Commission on 
Labour to suggest rationalisation of existing Labour Laws in the 
background of changing environment in view of liberalisation and 
reforms; 
(b) if so, the details thereof including the personnel of the 
Commission and its terms of reference; 
(c) the time allotted to it to submit its report; and 
(d) whether the Commission has be en adequately briefed to 
ensure minimum protection of workers and labour force both in the 
organised and unorganised sectors and if so, the details thereof; 
THE MINISTER OF LABOUR (DR. SATYA NARAYAN 
JATIYA): (a) to 
(d) A statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) to (d) Yes, Sir. The Government of India have set up a 
National Commission on Labour on 15.10.1999 under the Chairmanship 
of Shri Ravindra Varma. The Commission have been given 24 months 
to submit its report. The terms of  reference and composition of the 
Commission are given in the Statement I and II respectively. 
13 

RAJYA SABHA [23 November, 2000] 
Statement-I 
Terms of reference of the National Commission on Labour 
(i) to suggest rationalisation of existing laws relating to 
labour in the organised sector; and 
(ii) to suggest an umbrella legislation for ensuring a minimum 
level of protection to the workers in the unorganised 
sectors; 
In developing the frame-work for its recommendations, the 
Commission will take into account the following:—  
(i) follow up implications of the recommendations made by 
the Commission set up in May, 1998 for review of 
various administrative laws governing industry; 
(ii) the emerging economic environment involving rapid 
technological changes, requiring response in terms of change 
in methods, timings and conditions of work in industry, trade 
and services, globalisation of economy, liberlisation of trade 
and industry and emphasis on international competitiveness, 
and the need for bringing the existing laws in tune with the 
future labour market needs and demands; 
(iii) the minimum level of la bour protection and welfare 
measures and the basic institutional framework for 
ensuring the same, in a manner which is conducive to a 
flexible labour market and adjustments necessary for 
furthering technological change and economic growth; 
and 
(iv) improving the effectiveness of measures relating to social 
security, occupational health and safety, minimum wages 
and linkage of wages with productivity and in particular 
the safeguards and facilities required for-women and 
handicapped persons in employment.

Indo-American Relationship 
*67. SHRI CM. IBRAHIM: Will the Minister of EXTERNAL 
AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether on the eve of Prime Minister's visit to the United 
States, the US President indicated that he was looking forward to build 
permanent institutions to reflect th e depth of India and America's new 
relationship emerging from the exchange of visits between the US 
President and India's Prime Minister; 
30 

[23 November, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
(b) if so, the details of the permanent institutions contemplated by 
him and indicated to the Prime Minister during his US visit; and 
(c) the steps so far taken to build such institutions? 
THE MINISTER OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS (SHRI JASWANT 
SINGH): (a) India and the United States are working together to build 
a closer and qualitatively new rela tionship in the 21st century, as 
articulated by Prime Minister and Pr esident Clinton in their Vision 
Statement on 21st March, 2000 in Ne w Delhi. To give shape to this 
vision, the two sides have established an architecture of wide-ranging 
institutional dialogue between the two countries. The US President has 
stated that relations between India and the United States had moved in a 
new direction, and should be seen as a long-term effort, since it's 
"inconceivable...that we can build the kind of world we want over the 
next 10 to 20 years unless there is a very strong partnership between 
the United States and India." The two sides see the Dialogue 
Architecture in that context. 
(b) The Dialogue Architecture envisages regular "summits' 
between the Prime Minister of India and the US President. In addition, it 
includes ministerial level Foreign Policy Dialogue between EAM and 
US Secretary of State; a ministerial level Security Dialogue; Foreign 
Office Consultations and Asian Security Dialogue between Foreign 
Secretary and US Under Secretary of State; High Level Coordinating 
Group on Bilateral Economic Dialogue and ministerial level Indo-US 
Financial and Economic Forum, Indo-US Commercial Dialogue and 
Indo-US Working Group on Trade; Joint Working Group on Counter-
terrorism; Joint Working Group on Clean Energy and Environment; 
and, Indo-US Science & Technology Forum. During the visit of Prime 
Minister to the United States, the two sides agreed to establish an 
institutional dialogue on UN Peacekeeping Operations and set up a 
framework of bilateral dialogue on Afghanistan. 
(c) The two sides have implemented all the elements of the 
Dialogue Architecture. Following Prime Minister's visit to the US, the 
two sides have, in addition, established a Joint Working Group on UN 
Peacekeeping Operations. The two sides are currently in the process of 
institutionalising the dialogue on Afghanistan.

regard, precise estimates of the number of Indian citizens working as

however, work on the basis of a figure approximately of 1000 plus, as

The Government of India is not aware of any attempts to remove

them of facilities such as provident fund, increments, pension, voluntary 
retirement benefits, promotion, medi cal reimbursement, etc., benefits 
that are available to their Nepalese counterparts. 
The issue of regularisation of service of the Indian teachers in

including at the highest level. During the 
† Original notice of the question was received   in Hindi. 
45 

RAJYA SABHA [23 November, 2000] 
visit of the Prime Minister of Nepal to India in June 1990, it was agreed 
that the Indian national employed in schools in Nepal would be placed 
on the same footing as Nepalese nationals as regards the terms and 
conditions of employment. This assurance has been reiterated by the 
Nepalese side during subsequent high-level exchanges as well. 
In 1990-91, the Nepalese Cabinet had decided that as a one-time 
exception, all teachers who were wo rking for at least five years in 
various Government schools till the previous year, would be made 
permanent. In accordance with this decision, it is estimated that about 
100 Indian teachers were made permanent. In 1998, His Majesty's 
Government of Nepal issued a notification whereby the Indian teachers 
working in Nepalese schools, who have completed one year of service 
by 1990-91 and have still been working on temporary basis, would not 
be removed on the basis of nationality alone. The notification also 
stated that those teachers would like to retire or who voluntarily quit their 
position or who were removed for re asons other than nationality, shall 
be granted a lumpsum benefit depending on their length of service. 
The issue was again raised with the Prime Minister of Nepal, Mr. 
G. P. Koirala, during his visit to India in August 2000. A Joint Press 
Statement issued on August, 3,2000 during the visit stated that His 
Majesty's Government would implement the decisions taken in 1998 in 
this regard. Meanwhile, the Government of Indian continues to take up 
specific problems of the Indian teachers with His Majesty's Government 
of Nepal through diplomatic channels.

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF 
AGRICULTURE (SHRI SHRIPAD  YESSO NAIK) : (a) Yes, Sir.

(b) and (c) Generally, the fertility of soils improves with

and soil test based balanced and integrated nutrient management 
through conjunctive use of both inorganic and organic sources of plant 
nutrients to restore soil fertility. 
The Department of Agriculture and Cooperation is implementing 
various land based programmes, namely (i) Soil conservation in the 
catchments of River Valley Projects (RVP) and Flood Prone Rivers 
(FPR), (ii) Watershed Developmen t Project in Shifting Cultivation 
Areas, (iii) National Wa tershed Development Project in Rainfed Areas 
and (iv) Reclamation of Alkali Soil s, to minimise land degradation 
which ultimately results in enhanced fertility in the agricultural land of

385. SHRI PREM CHAND GUPTA: Will the Minister of 
CONSUMER AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION be

(a) whether it is a fact that Government had inadequate grain 
storage facilities to stock die foodgr ain produced, as a result of which 
it had to be dumped on the market at lower prices or even lying at 
various locations without proper storage facilities leading to pilferage

CONSUMER AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION (SHRI 
SRIRAM CHAUHAN): (a) to (c) There is no serious problem for storage

have formulated a National Policy on storage, handling and 
transportation of foodgrains which ai ms at harnessing the resources of 
public and private sectors, bom domestic and foreign, to build and 
operate infrastructure in bulk hand ling, storage and transportation of 
foodgrains in the country. Under this policy, the private sector will 
also be encouraged to build conventional godowns in which they will 
store and maintain foodgrains procured by Government agencies, for 
which they will be entitled to storage charges.

(SHRI MUNI LALL): (a) to (d) As per the 1991 Census Andhra Pradesh has

The Government have taken various steps to identify and

with Dist. Collectors and Project Directors of NCLPs and State Labour 
Secretaries / Labour Commissioners.

is one of the major programmes for education and rehabilitation of child 
labour in the country, evaluation of identified NCLPs was undertaken by 
evaluation agencies in the States of Uttar Pradesh, Tamil Nadu, Andhra 
Pradesh, Orissa and Rajasthan. Evaluation was also undertaken by Inter-

India and the planning process as practiced, has been one of the pillars of 
our approach to economic development and growth since 
independence and has stood us in good stead. We can take justifiable 
pride in having successfully reversed the worst inequities of our colonial 
heritage arid building a nation of considerable economic strength in a 
framework of democracy and federalism. The planning process 
culminates in the formulation of Five Year Plans which in turn are

the middle of our Ninth Five Year Plan. The growth in GDP realized in each of 
the last eight Five Year Plans, except for the Third Plan (1961—1966) and the 
Fourth Plan (1969—74), was almost as projected or above the projection in the 
respective Plan. 
The process of Plan formulation involves as well defined consultative 
mechanism that uses inputs and suggestions from structured consultations with 
diverse interest groups and professionals from various fields including 
education, agriculture, industry, services academics and voluntary

The seven Basic Services identified for priority attention were: 
1. 100 per cent coverage of provision of safe drinking water in 
rural and urban areas. 
2. 100 per cent coverage of primary health service facilities in 
rural and urban areas. 
3. Universalisation of primary education. 
4. Provision of Public Housing Assistance to all shelterless poor 
families. 
5. Supplementary Nutrition via Extension of Mid-Day Meal 
Programme in primary schools to all rural blocks and urban 
slums and disadvantaged sections and supplementary nutrition 
programme implemented as part of ICDS. 
6. Provision of connectivity to all unconnected villages and 
habitations. 
7. Streamlining of the Public Dist ribution System with a focus 
on the poor.

PUBLIC GRIEVANCES OF THE MINISTRY OF PERSONNEL, PUBLIC 
GRIEVANCES AND PENSIONS (SHRI ARUN SHOURIE): (a) to (c) The 
Planning Commission estimates poverty at national and state level from the 
large sample surveys on consumer expenditure conducted by die National 
Sample Survey Organization (NSSO) at an interval of approximately five 
years. The last such survey was conducted in 1993-94. The full data from 
next large survey on consumer expenditure conducted during the period July, 
1999 to June, 2000 are under process. As such, the estimates of poverty 
since the initiation of the policies of globalisation and economic reforms in 
1991, is available only for the year 1993-94. Hence, it is not possible to 
ascertain the change in poverty during the period of economic reforms. 
However, comparing two latest esti mates, 1987-88 and 1993-94, it is 
observed that the percentage of people living below the poverty line 
declined by 2.9 percentage points. 
(d) Broadly, die programmes and schemes initiated to eliminate 
poverty and remove social and economic disparities fall under two 
categories. These are: (a) self-employment programmes aimed at direct 
income generation for the poor through asset building, bypassing the 
general growth process, and (b) wage employment programmes. Since the 
Sixth Five Year Plan (1980—85), the Government has been implementing 
these programmes. Integrated Rural Development Programme (IRDP) 
has been the major self-employment programme and it has been in 
operation in all the blocks of the country since 1980. The wage 
employment programme initially was National Rural Employment 
Programme (NREP) during the Sixth Plan period. In the Seventh Plan, 
another wage employment programme under the name Rural Labour 
Employment Guarantee Programme (RLEGP) was introduced. Then in 
1989, Jawahar Rozgar Yojana (JRY) was launched by merging the National 
Rural Employment Programme and the Rural Labour Employment 
Guarantee Programme, and it beca me the main wage-employment 
programme. In addition, several programmes to help the poor were also in 
operation until March, 1999. These programmes are: Million Wells Scheme 
(MWS), Employment Assurance 
169 

RAJYA SABHA [23 November, 2000] 
Scheme (EAS), Development of Women and Children in Rural Areas 
(DWCRA), Training of Rural Youth for Self-Employment (TRYSEM), 
Supply of Improved Toolkits to Rural Artisans (SITRA). 
From 1st April, 1999, IRDP and allied programmes, alongwith 
Million Wells Scheme have been restructured into single self-employment 
programme called the Swarnajayanti Gram Swarozgar Yojana (SGSY) with 
the primary objectives of focussed approach to poverty alleviation. Jawahar 
Rozgar Yojana (JRY) has also been restructured as Jawahar Gram Samridhi 
Yojana (JGSY) with the primary objective of creation of demand driven 
community, village infrastructure including durable assets at the village 
level and assets to enable the rural poor to increase the opportunities for 
sustained employment. Its secondary objective is generation of 
supplementary employment for the unemployed poor in the rural areas. 
Employment Assurance Scheme has also been restructured from 1999- 
2000 to make it the single wage employment programme. While the basic 
parameters have been retained, the scheme has become allocative scheme 
instead of demand driven scheme and a fixed annual outlay is to be 
provided to the states. The wage employment under the programme is 
given to Below Poverty Lines (BPL) families. 
From 1.12.1997, Swama Jayanti Shahari Rozgar Yojana (SJSRY) is 
the main poverty alleviation programme in the urban areas. The SJSRY, 
which has subsumed all the earlier three urban poverty alleviation 
programmes, viz., Nehru Rozgar Yojana (NRY), Urban Basic Services for 
the Poor (UBSP) and Prime Minister's Integrated Urban Poverty Eradication 
Programme (PMIUPEP), seeks to provide gainful employment to urban 
unemployed or underemployed poor through encouraging the setting up of 
self employment ventures or provision of wage employment. The 
implementation of SJSRY is relying on suitable community structures on 
the UBSP pattern and delivery of inputs under this programme is through 
the medium of Urban Local Bodies (ULBs) and such community 
structure.

Revival of SSI Sector Under the Liberalisation Policy 
500. PROF. M.M. AGARWAL: Will the Minister of SMALL 
SCALE INDUSTRIES AND AGRO AND RURAL INDUSTRIES be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have formulated any specific policy for 
revival of small scale industries sector from the multinational 
companies being set up under die liberalisation policy; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; and 
(c) what effective measures are being contemplated by Government 
so as to revive our small scale sector in the changing scenario of economic 
reforms in the country? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE INDEPENDENT CHARGE) IN 
THE MINISTRY OF SMALL SCALE INDUSTRIES AND AGRO 
AND RURAL INDUSTRIES (SHRIMATI VASUNDHARA RAJE): (a) 
to (c) The policy of Government is to support the growth and development 
of the small scale sector in the coun try alongwith liberalisation of the 
economy. In this context, a number of measures have already been taken 
to promote the revival and rehabilitation of sick units. These include, 
inter alia, institutional mechanism in the form of State Level Inter 
Institutional committees, special rehabilitation cells in banks and State 
Financial Institutions and elaborate guidelines issued by Reserve Bank 
of India for extending rehabilitation assistance to eligible units. RBI has 
also announced a Samadhan Scheme on 27th July 2000, for one time 
settlement of SSI dues. In addition, as a follow up of die policy package for 
SSIs announced on 30th, 31st August, 2000, RBI has been requested to 
draw up detailed, transparent and non discretionary guidelines for 
rehabilitation of currently, sick but potentially viable SSI units.

is the status of the people in the Third World countries? Four 
billion people, two-thirds of the world population, are in acute 
poverty, ever enhancing unemployment and uncontrollabfe 
diseases. That is a very pitiable position globalisation has 
inflicted on the people. Take, for example, our own experience. 
Who can deny that our agricultural sector has been ruined by 
the liberated imports? Our key sectors are controlled by the 
corporates and international finance companies. Even the 
communications sector, the insurance, the banking and finance 
sectors are controlled by them. The villages are forgotten. The 
agriculturists are forgotten. The vast majority of agricultural

Minister to the United States, which has been repeatedly 
trumpeted as art achievement of the Government, we repeatedly 
went on record -- we found from newspaper reports -- to say that 
Jammu and Kashmir is not on the official agenda of the Summit. 
278 

[23 November, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
And yet, the U.S. President raised this issue, and our 
Prime Minister did not decisivel y tick him off, or, politely and 
firmly tell him that this is not the issue. Then, you have the 
spectacle of the MEA saying that this has found a very 
honourable mention in the joint communique. If that was the 
fact, Madam, why then did they say that it was not going to be 
on the agenda at all? They could have decisively raised it on 
the agenda and made sure that we have a statement in the 
communique. That would have been far more useful and 
satisfactory to India. Therefore, what we want to know, what this 
House wants to know and what the people of India want to 
know, is whether the foreign policy of India is determined in the 
South Block or by the khakil 
Madam, the second issue that I would like to raise is 
that, during the visit of the Prime Minister to the United States, 
our hon. Foreign Minister came here and told Parliament -- and 
what they did was a very good achievement, had it been 
implemented -- that an Extradition Treaty has been signed with 
:he United States, and this will help us to counter terrorism. Yet 
the fact is that, despite this Extradition Treaty having been 
signed, despite two meetings of the Indo-U.S. Working Group 
on Terrorism, which is supposed to be a signal achievement of 
this Government, the Government of India failed to achieve the 
extradition of even one terrorist --I would like the Minister to 
explain whether it is a fact that not even the name of one 
terrorist has been submitted to the U.S.A. for extradition. 
Therefore, what is the purpose of this treaty of extradition, and 
what have we achieved after two meetings of this Group, is 
something beyond my comprehension. Therefore, I would like 
the Minister of Foreign Affairs to kindly explain the stand of the 
Government in this regard. 
Madam, this abnegation of independence of thought and 
action, which is the essence of our non-aligned policy, is 
nowhere more evident than in our present stand on Palestine. 
Palestine has never been a non-Indian issue. Our Minister of 
Foreign Affairs is a very learned person. He has been in 
Parliament for years. Nobody knows it better than him, but as 
far as the Government is concerned, I doubt whether the 
Government is aware that Palestine has never been a non-
Indian issue. In fact, this dimension, since the Belford 
Declaration of 1917, has been an integral part of our freedom 
struggle and this is something that is of immense sentimental 
value to the people of India. Mahatma Gandhi proclaimed that 
Palestine belonged to Palestine, and as England did to the 
English, and France to the French. Therefore, when the British 
mandate ended and the future of Palestine came 
279 

RAJYA SABHA        [23 November, 2000] 
up before the United Nations in 1947, we opposed the partition 
of Palestine, as we opposed other partitions. And, 50 years after 
Palestine was partitioned, it is as clear in West Asia as it is in 
Ireland, Cyprus, Rwanda or Burundi, and anywhere in South 
Asia, that partition is no solution to anything. This is why we 
never agreed, Madam, with the call of the Arabs to throw the 
Jews into the sea or with the Zionist claim that Palestine is a 
land without people or people without land. This is why we took 
a serious note of terrorism itself, pleading with the colonial 
powers that Israel is an agent, it should be recognised as an 
agent of imperialism in Asia. And that is why, as a signatory to 
the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, we champion the 
rights of the millions of Palestinians who were driven out of 
Palestine. 
Madam, I am aware of the paucity of time, and I would 
just state two or three other points that I want to bring to your 
notice, because this is a matter of serious concern to me. The 
Minister of External Affairs said - he will correct me, if I am 
wrong; I would like to beg the pardon of the House, if I am 
quoting him wrongly -- he quoted in Jerusalem itself that India's 
Palestine policy, till date, had been driven by the Muslim vote 
bank. If such was the statement he made -- I can be corrected, 
if I am wrong -- he has insulted the 80 years of solidarity that we 
have with the Arab world. Then, it means, Madam, 
communalism is now replacing non-alignment as the basis of 
South Block's foreign policy. No Wonder, Madam, then that 
alarm and confusion prevail all over the Arab world. 
Then, no wonder that an alarming confusion prevailed 
all over the Arab world and all over the non-alligned world about 
India's stand on the Palestine issue. The ugly fact of the matter 
is that the Government of India is interested, perhaps, in playing 
second fiddle to the Americans and not in asserting the 
independence of our West Asian stand. 
Further proof of our drift from the Non-Alligned 
Movement is evident from the unequal treatment meted out to 
President Clinton and President Putin, who followed him 
immediately. We welcomed President Clinton's visit. Madam, but 
his visit resembled that of an imperial progress through a 
country, somewhat like the progress of the Romans; whereas, 
the other Heads-of State and governments who visited India, 
were not given the same treatment at all, and it is unexplicable 
to me, at least. 
Why did our hon. Prime Minister choose this lameduck 
administration to visit the U.S.? It was clear to everybody that 
President 
280 

[23 November, 2000) RAJYA SABHA 
Clinton was coming to India and no substantive announcements 
of foreign policy could be made by the lameduck administration. 
It was very clear that there would be a new person, either Mr. 
Gore or Mr. Bush, sitting in the White House. It would have 
been far more meaningful if we had waited for that government 
to take office, before visiting the U.S., during a lameduck 
administration. 
This is in startling and striking contrast to the visit of my 
late leader, Rajiv Gandhi, to China. He made a clear declaration 
of a tremendous change in Indo-China Policy and it was after 
three years' assiduous preparations that he visited China, which 
is the reason why there has been a steady improvement in the 
ties between India and China. Why such preparations could not 
have been made before our Prime Minister's visit to the U.S.? 
Why did he go in haste and visit the lameduck administration? 
This is something important which our Foreign Minister should 
explain. 
Madam, nothing has come out of this visit. With great 
respect to our respectable Prime Minister, I would say that 
nothing has come out of the visit and nothing has happened on 
the sanctions front. Nothing has happened on the question of 
India's nuclear policy in our favour and nothing has happened 
on the question of a permanent seat for India in the Security 
Council. All that has happened was the delivery of yet another 
homily to us regarding Kashmir and regarding our nuclear stand 
by President Clinton. Indeed, one thing happened. We signed 
an agreement for one lakh extra visas for our countrymen to go 
there. Out of one lakh visas, I do not know whether even one 
person has gone so far. It will take some time. In fact, the 
prospective President, either Bush or Gore, who would be 
sitting over there, is the person who is going to issue the visas. 
It would have been far more sensible if our Prime Minister had 
visited the U.S. after the new government had taken over. 
Lastly, Madam, on the Kargil issue, the Subrahmanyam 
report is yet to be debated. Kargil issue is not just a matter of 
defence; it is something much more. I say this without 
hesitation that when the Prime Minister went on a bus to 
Lahore, all of us felt very happy. We lauded the statesmanship 
of his great experience and we thought that this was a 
departure and it was going to be a new type of BJP 
Government, which we did not expect. We thought that there 
was going to be a tremendous breakthrough in Indo-Pakistan 
relationship; but, then, we did not realise that it was actually a 
theatre of the absurd because on that very day, the massacre 
took place in the Kargil sector made it into a theatre of the

absurd. It caused the death of so many of our brave jawans 
and there was mindless maiming and physical impairment of
